merged.title: Fix buffer leak in ProtobufDecoder on cancel
merged.body:
`ProtobufDecoder.decode(Publisher)` releases the buffer of a partially read message with `doOnTerminate`, so only when the input completes or fails. When the subscriber cancels while a message is split across data buffers, for example right after receiving the previous message, that buffer is never released. With pooled buffers, such as Netty's, it leaks.

This change uses `doFinally` instead, as `AbstractCharSequenceDecoder` does, so that the buffer is also released on cancel.

The new `ProtobufDecoderTests#decodeCancelWhileMessageIncomplete` decodes a data buffer that holds one message and half of the next, then cancels after the first message. Without the change, `LeakAwareDataBufferFactory` reports 1 buffer leak. The protobuf codec tests of `spring-web` and checkstyle pass.

merged.title: Respect logger-name hierarchy boundary in LoggerNameLevelRewritePolicy
merged.body:
Fixes #4412

`rewrite()` matched the configured logger name with `String.startsWith`, so a policy configured for `"com.foo"` also incorrectly matched an unrelated sibling package such as `"com.foobar.Baz"`, which merely shares the same character prefix without being a sub-logger of it.

This is inconsistent with every other logger-name-hierarchy feature in Log4j (e.g. `<Logger name="com.foo">` configuration, which resolves by progressively truncating at the last dot, not by substring matching), and it silently rewrites/demotes log levels for packages the operator never intended to affect — a `WARN` from `com.foobar.Baz` could be silently demoted to `DEBUG` by a rule meant only for `com.foo`.

Fix: require an exact match or a genuine `.`-separated descendant, matching the hierarchy semantics used everywhere else in the project.

Added `LoggerNameLevelRewritePolicyTest.testPrefixMatchRespectsLoggerHierarchyBoundary` covering the sibling-package false match, the true child-logger case, and the exact-match case.

`./mvnw test` for the `rewrite` package is green aside from one pre-existing, unrelated failure in `RewriteAppenderTest` that also reproduces on an unmodified checkout (confirmed before writing this, so it's not something this change introduced).

Changelog entry included under `src/changelog/.2.x.x/`.

merged.title: Fix #134: Add a FAQ entry for "Got bad greeting from SMTP host"
merged.body:

This adds a FAQ entry, right after the "Must issue a STARTTLS command first" one, for:

```
Got bad greeting from SMTP host: <host>, port: <port>, response: [EOF]
```

As requested in the issue, it explains:

merged.title: Fix #456: Do not call toString() of an object whose setter fails
merged.body:
Fixes #456.

**What**

#570 fixed the getter half of #456 in `ValueGetterSerializer`: the message of a failing getter names the class of the object instead of calling its `toString()`. The setter half is still there. When a setter throws during `fromJson`, `ValueSetterDeserializer` builds its message with `"Error setting value on: " + object`, which calls `toString()` on an object that is only partially deserialized.

If that `toString()` fails, its exception replaces the setter's. For example, a setter that throws `IllegalArgumentException("invalid IBAN")`, in a class whose `toString()` dereferences a field that is not set yet, currently gives:

```
jakarta.json.bind.JsonbException: Internal error: Cannot invoke "String.toUpperCase()" because "this.owner" is null
```

and the `IllegalArgumentException` is not in the cause chain at all.

**How**

`ValueSetterDeserializer` now uses the class name of the instance in the message, like `ValueGetterSerializer`, and keeps the setter's exception as the cause. The name is `null` if there is no instance, which can happen if a `@JsonbCreator` factory method returns `null`, so that the original exception is not replaced by a second `NullPointerException` in that case either.

merged.title: Document the order of application and profile specific files
merged.body:
Fixes #1868

The Environment Repository page explains the precedence rules in general terms. It does not say where a file named after both the application and a profile, such as `foo-dev.yml`, ranks against `application-dev.yml`, `foo.yml` and `application.yml`. The issue asks exactly that.

This adds an ordered list for the page's sample client (`foo` with the `dev` and `mysql` profiles), from the highest precedence to the lowest:

1. `foo-mysql.yml`
2. `application-mysql.yml`
3. `foo-dev.yml`
4. `application-dev.yml`
5. `foo.yml`
6. `application.yml`

The list is scoped to native, Git and SVN repositories and to one search location. Those backends build a `NativeEnvironmentRepository`, which sets `spring.config.name` to `application,{application}`, so Spring Boot's rules give this order. I did not check the S3 backend, which builds its `Environment` differently.

### Testing

`NativeEnvironmentRepositoryTests` gets a test with the six files in one classpath location. It asserts the order of the property sources for an `orders` application with the `dev,mysql` profiles, and that the first one is `orders-mysql.yml`. It pins existing behaviour, so it passed on the first run. `./mvnw -pl spring-cloud-config-server -am verify -Dtest=NativeEnvironmentRepositoryTests` passes, including Checkstyle and the Spring Java Format check.

merged.title: Try the next config server URI after an unreadable response
merged.body:
See #1723

When a config server answers with a body that the client cannot read as an `Environment`, such as an HTML page, `RestTemplate` throws an `UnknownContentTypeException`. Before this change, that exception stopped the client at the first URI, even with `multiple-uri-strategy: always`, while a 4xx or 5xx response moved on to the next URI.

With this change, `ConfigServerConfigDataLoader` and the bootstrap `ConfigServicePropertySourceLocator` try the next URI after an unreadable response when the strategy is `always`, and log it at INFO like the other failures. The last URI, or any URI with `connection-timeout-only`, rethrows the `UnknownContentTypeException` as before, so fail fast and optional imports behave as they did.

Following the review, the first version's message, which pointed at the credentials for an HTML response and included the config server URI, is gone.

### Testing

Test first: the `always` tests failed on `main` with `ConfigClientFailFastException`, because the client stopped at the first URI.

- `ConfigServerConfigDataLoaderTests` and `ConfigServicePropertySourceLocatorTests`: the first URI answers `200` with `text/html`. With `always`, the second URI is used. With `connection-timeout-only`, fail fast reports the `UnknownContentTypeException` as the cause.
- `./mvnw -pl spring-cloud-config-client verify` passes, including Checkstyle and the Spring Java Format check.

merged.title: Fix #104: Send IMAP search text in UTF-8 when UTF8=ACCEPT is enabled
merged.body:
Fixes #104.

**What**

When the server advertises `UTF8=ACCEPT`, `IMAPStore` enables it after login (RFC 6855). `IMAPProtocol.search()` then sends the `SEARCH` command without a `CHARSET`, as the RFC requires, through `issueSearch(msgSequence, term, null)`. But `issueSearch()` also passes the `null` charset to `SearchSequence.generateSequence()`, so `Argument.writeString(String)` writes the text with `ASCIIUtility.getBytes()`, which keeps only the low byte of each character. A subject term such as `ä` or `ü` reaches the server as invalid UTF-8, and the server rejects the command. As the issue describes, `IMAPFolder` then falls back to searching on the client, fetching every message of the folder, which takes minutes on a large mailbox.

**How**

As suggested in the issue comments, `issueSearch()` generates the search sequence with UTF-8 when no charset is given and UTF-8 has been enabled. The command is still sent without `CHARSET`. Without UTF-8 support nothing changes: ASCII text is still sent as is, and non-ASCII text still goes through the `SEARCH CHARSET` attempts in `search()`.

With UTF-8 enabled, `Argument` writes text that contains non-ASCII characters as a quoted string, never as an atom, which RFC 6855 section 3 allows once `ENABLE UTF8=ACCEPT` has been sent. Text with CR or LF, or longer than 1024 bytes, is still sent as a literal. Since the charset is passed down to `SearchSequence`, the subject, from, recipient, header and body terms are all encoded the same way

merged.title: Fix #652: Apply a class adapter to values of a type known at runtime
merged.body:
Fixes #652.

**What**

An adapter declared with `@JsonbTypeAdapter` on a class is ignored when an instance is serialized as an element of a collection whose element type is not known statically, such as `List.of(c)` or `Set.of(c)`. The element is written field by field instead:

```java
jsonb.toJson(List.of(new AnnotatedType())); // [{"field":"value"}] instead of ["adapted"]
jsonb.toJson(new AnnotatedType());          // {"field":"value"} after the call above, "adapted" before it
```

As the issue shows, the result also depends on the order. The serializer built for the element is cached for the class, so a later `toJson()` of the object itself ignores the adapter too. An adapter registered with `JsonbConfig.withAdapters` works in both cases.

**Why**

The element type of a raw collection is `Object`, so its serializer is an `ObjectTypeSerializer`. That serializer resolves the runtime class through `SerializationModelCreator.serializerChainRuntime()`, passing the customization of the declared type, `Object`. `ComponentMatcher.getSerializeAdapterBinding()` finds no adapter in that customization and none in the configuration, so the class-level annotation, which lives in the `ClassCustomization` of the runtime class, is never looked at. For a root value, `serializerChain()` uses the class customization of the value's type, which is why `toJson(c)` alone works.

**How**

`serializerChainRuntime()` keeps the given customization when it binds a serializer or an adapter. Otherwise

merged.title: Fix #155, #201: Send a long SMTP initial response after the challenge
merged.body:
Fixes #155 and #201.

**What**

The SMTP provider always sends the initial response of a mechanism with the `AUTH` command. With XOAUTH2 the initial response contains the access token,, and tokens of a thousand characters or more occur, for example with Google Workspace domain-wide delegation as in #201. The command line then exceeds the SMTP limit of 512 octets including CRLF (RFC 5321, section 4.5.3.1.4), and servers reject it:

- `500 5.5.2 Line too long` in #155, with SASL;
- `555-5.5.2 Syntax error, command line too long` from Google in #201, through the Jenkins email-ext plugin.

RFC 4954, section 4, covers this case: if the initial response would make the `AUTH` command exceed the line length limit, the client must not send it with the command. It must send `AUTH <mechanism>` alone and give the response in reply to the server's first, empty `334` challenge, a line that has no such limit.

**How**

- `SMTPTransport.fitsAuthCommand(mech, ir)` checks whether `AUTH <mech> <ir>` fits in 510 characters, which is the 512 octets without the CRLF.
- `SMTPTransport.Authenticator.authenticate()`, used by PLAIN, XOAUTH2 and the other built-in mechanisms, and `SMTPSaslAuthenticator.authenticate()` both defer an initial response that does not fit. They send `AUTH <mech>`, then the initial response in reply to the first `334`. What follows is unchanged, including the `530`/STARTTLS retry.
- An initial response that fits is still sent with the command as before, so nothing changes for

merged.title: Fix #165: Do not modify the response when parsing a quoted string
merged.body:
Fixes #165.

**What**

`Response.parseString()` removes the escape characters of a quoted string by shifting the bytes of the response buffer in place. A comment there already warned that this is a destructive copy. The buffer is shared by every copy of the response, because the `Response(Response)` copy constructor keeps the same array. `IMAPProtocol` creates a `FetchResponse` for each FETCH response, and further `FetchResponse`s can be built from the same `IMAPResponse`. Once one of them has read the quoted string, the others see the shifted bytes.

For the Gmail label from the issue, `* 1 FETCH (X-GM-LABELS ("\\Sent" CustomLabel) ...)`:

- the first parse returns `\Sent`, which is correct, and leaves `"\Sentt"` in the buffer, so `toString()` shows `("\Sentt" CustomLabel)`;
- any later parse of the same bytes returns `Sentt`.

This is why parsing a fresh `IMAPResponse` once, as in the test in the issue's comments, does not reproduce it.

**How**

When a quoted string contains escape characters, `parseString()` unescapes it into a new array and returns that, as a `String` or a `ByteArray`. The response buffer is left unchanged. A quoted string without escape characters is still returned as a view of the buffer, without copying.

**Tests**

- reading `"\\Sent"`, resetting and reading it again;
- reading it from a copy of the response after the original read it;
- reading a quoted string with escapes as a `ByteArray`, which checks the unescaped

merged.title: Fix #609: Reject a JSON array or object where a value is expected
merged.body:
Fixes #609.

**What**

Since Yasson 3, a JSON array bound to a scalar property is accepted silently, as the issue describes. For `{"test": ["data1", "data2", "data3", "data4"]}` and a `String test` property, `fromJson` returns `test = "data4"`. Yasson 2 threw `Can't deserialize JSON array into: class java.lang.String`. The same happens for an `Integer` property, and for an array of objects bound to an object property.

**Why**

`PositionChecker` checks that the parser is at an event expected for the type. If it is not, it advances the parser by one event, which is meant for user-defined deserializers that leave the parser just before the value. When the parser is at `START_ARRAY`, that step enters the array, so the first element is read as the value. The checker only verifies the closing event for a container it expected, and the enclosing object deserializer then reads the remaining elements as further values for the same property, so the last one wins.

**How**

`PositionChecker` no longer advances into an array or an object that is not one of the expected events. The document is rejected with the existing `JsonbException`, for example:

```
Unable to deserialize property 'value' because of: Incorrect position for processing type: class java.lang.String. Received event: START_ARRAY Allowed: [...]
```

The skip still applies to every other event, so user-defined deserializers that call `DeserializationContext.deserialize` before advancing to the value keep working.

merged.title: GH-8337: Add outbound header name patterns to the DefaultJmsHeaderMapper
merged.body:
Fixes #8337

The `DefaultJmsHeaderMapper` can already restrict the JMS properties mapped inbound with name patterns (the `DefaultJmsHeaderMapper(String...)` constructor), but outbound it copies every eligible message header to the JMS properties. The issue asks for a way to keep some headers out of the JMS message, which today needs a `HeaderFilter` in front of the JMS endpoint (the workaround mentioned in the issue).

## What it adds

- `DefaultJmsHeaderMapper.setOutboundHeaderNames(String...)`, with the same pattern syntax as the inbound property names: simple wildcards and `!` negation, the first pattern that matches a header name decides (`PatternMatchUtils.smartMatch`, as for the inbound side). For instance `"!internal*", "*"` maps everything except the `internal*` headers.
- The patterns are matched against the header names, before the `outboundPrefix` is added.
- The default is `"*"`, so all the eligible headers are still mapped, and the JMS API headers (`jms_correlationId`, `jms_replyTo`, `jms_type`) are mapped regardless of the patterns.
- A paragraph with an example in the JMS header mapping section, and an entry in the 7.2 what's new. I used `@since 7.2`; I can change it to 7.3 if it does not make it into this cycle.

merged.title: Fix the local antora task
merged.body:
`./gradlew antora`, which the `CONTRIBUTING.md` documents for building the reference documentation, fails on `main` (I ran into it while working on #3728). The published documentation is not affected, since it is built from the `docs-build` branch.

There are two problems:

1. The `clean`, `fetch` and `stacktrace` options are `'true'` strings. The Antora Gradle plugin turns a string value into an argument after the option, so the command ends with three extra `true` arguments:

   ```
   antora: too many arguments for 'generate'. Expected 1 argument but got 4.
   ```

   This PR passes them as booleans, so they become plain flags, as `spring-integration` does.

2. Once the site is generated, the build still fails with the configuration cache, because the Antora Gradle plugin `1.0.0` brings the Node Gradle plugin `3.5.1`, which starts an external process during the configuration:

   ```
   - Plugin class 'com.github.gradle.node.NodePlugin': external process started 'uname -m'
   ```

   This PR declares the Node Gradle plugin `7.1.0` (in the version catalog, `apply false`), which supports the configuration cache and is used instead of `3.5.1` on the build classpath.

With both changes, `./gradlew antora` generates the site in `build/site`, stores the configuration cache entry, and a second run reuses it. I checked this locally on macOS with JDK 25. `./gradlew help` still configures the whole build.

merged.title: FELIX-6861 Propagate IOExceptions of stream handlers invoked reflectively
merged.body:
Fixes [FELIX-6861](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/FELIX-6861).

`URLHandlersStreamHandlerProxy.openConnection(URL)` and `openConnection(URL, Proxy)` invoke a stream handler that is not a `URLStreamHandlerService` of the framework class loader (the built-in handler, or a handler from another class loader) through reflection. `Method.invoke()` wraps an `IOException` thrown by the handler in an `InvocationTargetException`, which the generic `catch (Exception)` then wrapped in an `IllegalStateException("Stream handler unavailable due to: null")`. So `URL.openConnection()` failures such as `FileNotFoundException` escaped `catch (IOException)` blocks, unlike with a direct invocation of the handler.

A small `rethrowIOException()` helper now rethrows the handler's `IOException` (the cause of the `InvocationTargetException`) on the four reflective paths:

- the reflective invocation in `openConnection(URL)` and in `openConnection(URL, Proxy)`;
- the extension handler branch of `openConnection(URL)`, which wrapped it in a new `IOException` without the original type or stack;
- the reflective call of `openConnection(URL, Proxy)` on a `URLStreamHandlerService`, which did the same.

Other invocation failures keep their current handling (`IllegalStateException` or `IOException` as before).

merged.title: Fix #627: Reuse registered serializer and deserializer instances
merged.body:
Fixes #627.

`ComponentMatcher.introspectSerializerBinding()` and `introspectDeserializerBinding()` are documented to reuse the instance registered in the context for the same type ("If an instance of serializerClass is present in context and is bound for same type, return that instance"), but they compare `componentBindings.getSerializer().getClass()`, which is `SerializerBinding` (resp. `DeserializerBinding`), with the serializer class, so the check never matches. `introspectAdapterBinding()` compares `getAdapterInfo().getAdapter().getClass()`, the wrapped component, and works.

The visible effect: a property annotated with `@JsonbTypeSerializer(X.class)` / `@JsonbTypeDeserializer(X.class)` always gets a new instance of `X` from the component instance creator, even when an instance of `X` configured with `JsonbConfig.withSerializers()` / `withDeserializers()` is bound for the same type. A stateful or specially constructed instance is ignored, and every annotated property creates its own instance.

The two checks now compare the class of the wrapped serializer / deserializer (`getJsonbSerializer()` / `getJsonbDeserializer()`).

**Test:** `RegisteredComponentReuseTest` registers a serializer and a deserializer whose output depends on how they were constructed, and checks that an annotated property uses the registered instances, and still gets a new instance when none is registered. merged.title: Fix #651: Support TIME_IN_MILLIS and locale-only @JsonbDateFormat on creator parameters
merged.body:
Fixes #651.

`AnnotationIntrospector.getConstructorDateFormatter()` passes the value of `@JsonbDateFormat` to `DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern()` unconditionally, including the `JsonbDateFormat.TIME_IN_MILLIS` (`##time-in-millis`) and `JsonbDateFormat.DEFAULT_FORMAT` (`##default`) markers. So deserializing a record component or a `@JsonbCreator` parameter annotated with `@JsonbDateFormat(TIME_IN_MILLIS)`, or with only a locale such as `@JsonbDateFormat(locale = "de")`, fails with:

```
jakarta.json.bind.JsonbException: Internal error: Pattern includes reserved character: '#'
```

The property path (`createJsonbDateFormatter()`) already treats these two values as markers rather than patterns and creates a `JsonbDateFormatter(format, locale)` without a `DateTimeFormatter`, so that the date converters use epoch millis or their default formats. The creator parameter path now does the same.

**Test:** `RecordTest.testRecordWithDateFormats` deserializes and serializes a record with a `TIME_IN_MILLIS` `Instant`, a locale-only `LocalDate` and a plain `Instant`. On `main` it fails with the exception above; with the change it passes, and `mvn verify -Pcheckstyle,copyright` passes locally.

merged.title: Issue #14127 - Deploy directories whose names contain dots
merged.body:
Fixes #14127.

**What**

`DeploymentScanner.pathsChanged()` groups the scanned paths into apps by `FileID.getBasename(path)`, which drops everything after the last dot, for directories too. So a webapp directory `foo.com/` became the app `foo`, separate from the app `foo.com` of `foo.com.properties` (or `foo.com.xml`/`foo.com.war`), which is the two apps seen in the debug log of the issue: `foo` with only the directory and `foo.com` with only the properties file.

The code after it was meant to strip `.d` from nominated directories, but `FileID.isExtension(Path, ...)` is always `false` for directories (`getExtension(Path)` returns `null` for anything but a regular file), so that branch never ran; `foo.d/` only ended up in the app `foo` because `getBasename()` dropped `.d` as an extension.

**How**

A new `toBasename(Path)` gives the app basename of a scanned path:

- a file: its name without extension, as before (`foo.war`, `foo.xml`, `foo.com.properties` → `foo`, `foo`, `foo.com`);
- a directory: its whole name (`foo.com/` → `foo.com`), as directories have no extension, matching the documented pairing of `foo/` with `foo.war`/`foo.xml`; a nominated directory drops its `.d` suffix (`foo.d/` → `foo`), now checked on the directory name;
- a path that no longer exists, such as a removed directory, which cannot be told apart from a file anymore: the app that already holds that path, so that removing `foo.com/` undeploys `foo.com`.

merged.title: Document the session-only PluginParameterExpressionEvaluator constructor
merged.body:
Fixes #8052 (MNG-6982).

`PluginParameterExpressionEvaluator` has a constructor taking only a `MavenSession`, but `evaluate()` starts with `mojoExecution.getMojoDescriptor()` for every `${...}` expression, so an evaluator created that way fails with a `NullPointerException` even for `${project}`, `${session}` or `${basedir}`.

The mojo descriptor is now looked up only when there is a mojo execution, and `${plugin}` / `${plugin.*}` evaluate to `null` without one, which is what `${mojo.*}` already did (`ReflectionValueExtractor.evaluate()` returns `null` for a `null` root) and what unknown expressions do, so the usual fallback to the properties still applies. The session-only constructor documents this.

`PluginParameterExpressionEvaluatorTest.testEvaluationWithoutMojoExecution` covers `${session}`, `${project}`, a literal, and the mojo and plugin expressions; it fails on `master` with the `NullPointerException` at the first `evaluate()`.

The same code is in `maven-core` on `maven-3.10.x` (the issue was reported against 3.6.3); a backport would be welcome if you agree with the change.

merged.title: GH-2392: Add batch declaration methods to the AmqpAdmin
merged.body:
Fixes #2392

`RabbitAdmin` already declares the exchanges, queues and bindings of the application context on a single channel (through its private `declareExchanges(Channel, Exchange...)`, `declareQueues(Channel, Queue...)` and `declareBindings(Channel, Binding...)`), but the programmatic API only exposes one object per call, each on its own channel. Gary was not against adding batch methods on the issue, provided the exception handling is thought through, so this is my proposal for it.

## What it adds

- `AmqpAdmin#declareExchanges(Exchange...)`, `#declareQueues(Queue...)` and `#declareBindings(Binding...)`, as `default` methods that declare one by one, so other implementations keep working.
- `RabbitAdmin` overrides them to declare all the objects on a single channel, reusing the existing private helpers. The exception handling is the one of the single declarations, applied per object: when `ignoreDeclarationExceptions` is `true` on the admin or on the object, a failure is logged, a `DeclarationExceptionEvent` is published and the next object is declared; otherwise the failure is rethrown and the remaining objects are not declared. A connection-level failure of the batch is reported the same way, with the objects listed in the log message. The objects are added to the manual declarables when `redeclareManualDeclarations` is set, as for the single declarations.

merged.title: GH-6485: Add proxy support to the FTP session factories
merged.body:
Fixes #6485

An FTP server behind a proxy could so far only be reached with the proxy system properties of the JVM (`socksProxyHost` and friends), which affect every connection of the application, or by writing a custom session factory. This adds the two options that Artem sketched on the issue.

## What it adds

- `AbstractFtpSessionFactory#setProxy(java.net.Proxy)`, so `DefaultFtpSessionFactory` and `DefaultFtpsSessionFactory` connect through a SOCKS proxy, or through an HTTP proxy with the `CONNECT` tunneling of the JVM. The proxy is passed to `FTPClient#setProxy()`, which makes the client use it for the control connection and for the passive data connections. Because the server cannot connect back to the client through a proxy, the factory requires `FTPClient.PASSIVE_LOCAL_DATA_CONNECTION_MODE` when a proxy is set, and fails fast with a message that says so.
- `FtpHttpProxySessionFactory`, based on `FTPHTTPClient`, for an HTTP proxy that requires credentials (sent with the basic scheme). It defaults to, and only accepts, the passive client mode. The name follows the `Default*SessionFactory` style; the issue mentioned `FtpHttpSessionFactory`, so please say if you prefer that one.
- Reference documentation (a "Proxy Support" section in the FTP session factory chapter) and a What's New entry.

## Testing

merged.title: Fix the formatting of instants before the epoch (#4399)
merged.body:
Fixes #4399.

Instants before the epoch were mishandled in two places, because a truncating `/` or `%` was used where a floor division is needed:

* `MutableInstant.initFromEpochMilli(long, int)` split a negative `epochMilli` with `/ 1000`, so `-61_500 ms` became `epochSecond=-61, nanoOfSecond=-500_000_000`. That breaks the `0 <= nanoOfSecond < 1_000_000_000` invariant that `initFromEpochSecond` enforces and every consumer expects. It now uses `Math.floorDiv`, which gives `epochSecond=-62, nanoOfSecond=500_000_000`.
* `InstantPatternDynamicFormatter` keyed its per-minute cache with `epochSecond / 60` and rendered the seconds with `epochSecond % 60`. Before the epoch the seconds were negative and the wrong cached minute was selected: `%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS}` printed `23:59:+'.000` for `-59_000 ms` instead of `23:59:01.000`. These now use `Math.floorDiv` and `Math.floorMod`.

Both methods exist since Java 8, so there is no change to the supported baseline. For instants after the epoch the results are identical, because floor and truncating division agree for non-negative operands.

Deliberately not included: `InstantPatternThreadLocalCachedFormatter` starts its cache with the epoch instant `-1`, so the first event on a thread at exactly second (or millisecond) `-1` prints an empty string. That is described under "Related" in #4399. I left it out because #4322 rewrites that class.

merged.title: Ignore Accept-Charset when reading String request bodies
merged.body:
`StringBodyReader` and `TextPlainObjectBodyReader` decoded the request body with `MessageBodyWriter.findCharset(mediaType, headers)`. When the `Content-Type` has no `charset`, that falls back to the `Accept-Charset` header, and for a request body the headers are the request's own. So `Content-Type: application/json` plus `Accept-Charset: Big5` made a UTF-8 body decode as Big5 and corrupted non-ASCII text.

`Accept-Charset` expresses preferences for the response (RFC 9110 section 12.5.2), not the encoding of the request body. The readers now use only the `charset` parameter of the `Content-Type`, falling back to the configured default charset (UTF-8 unless `micronaut.application.default-charset` is set).

Tests: `RequestBodyCharsetTest` covers buffer, InputStream and chunked reads with `Accept-Charset: Big5` and `ISO-8859-1`, a missing media type, `text/plain`, and that an explicit `Content-Type` charset still wins. On `5.2.x` nine of the eleven tests fail, with the garbled output from the report; the two guards for the explicit charset pass before and after.

Two notes for review:
- This changes behaviour for clients that relied on `Accept-Charset` to choose the request body charset when the `Content-Type` has none. That was never correct per the RFC, and it is what the issue asks for.
- `HttpMessage#getCharacterEncoding()` (via `HttpUtil.getCharset` and `HttpUtil.resolveCharset`) still falls back to the request's `Accept-Charset`, and `NettyHttpRequestSpec` asserts that on p

merged.title: Fix RV_RETURN_VALUE_IGNORED_NO_SIDE_EFFECT false negative for Arrays.copyOf
merged.body:
Fixes #3900

Ignoring the result of `Arrays.copyOf` / `Arrays.copyOfRange` was never reported. The allow-list in `FindNoSideEffectMethods` is not the cause: `copyOf` is already inferred to be pure from its bytecode, and `Arrays.binarySearch`, which *is* allow-listed, was not reported either.

The methods were lost in `report()`. `java.util.Arrays` uses `assert`, so javac gives it a static initializer calling `Class.desiredAssertionStatus()`. That call was taken for a side effect, so the initializer was recorded as side-effecting and every static method of the class was registered as `SE_CLINIT` ("maybe called only to trigger class initialization"), which `MethodReturnCheck` never reports. The same happened to the pure static methods and constructors of any analyzed class containing an `assert`.

Changes
- Treat `Class.desiredAssertionStatus()` as side-effect free (root cause).
- List `Arrays.copyOf` / `Arrays.copyOfRange` explicitly next to `binarySearch`: `copyOfRange` rejects an invalid range with an `IllegalArgumentException`, which the bytecode analysis takes for a side effect.
- Reproducer `spotbugsTestCases/.../ghIssues/Issue3900.java` + `Issue3900Test` covering copyOf/copyOfRange (int[] and Object[] overloads), a user class using `assert` (static method and constructor), and used-result negatives.

merged.title: add haveOnlyFinalNonSyntheticFields() to ignore synthetic fields
merged.body:
Some compilers create non-final synthetic fields, e.g. the Eclipse compiler generates a `$SWITCH_TABLE$...` field for every switch over an enum. `classes().should().haveOnlyFinalFields()` reported such fields as violations although they do not appear in the source code and cannot be declared `final` by the developer (see the discussion in the issue, where ignoring synthetic members in predefined predicates was suggested).

Keep `haveOnlyFinalFields()` exactly as it is and add `haveOnlyFinalNonSyntheticFields()` to `ArchConditions` and `ClassesShould` as an explicit alternative that ignores fields with modifier `SYNTHETIC`.
Link the alternative from the Javadoc of `haveOnlyFinalFields()`.

<details><summary>Initial plan (discarded)</summary>

> This PR excludes fields with modifier `SYNTHETIC` from `haveOnlyFinalFields()` only, leaving `haveOnlyPrivateConstructors()` and all other conditions untouched, since excluding synthetic members globally has proven problematic in the past. merged.title: Treat a null Request.Body as a request with no body
merged.body:
`Request.create(..., (Request.Body) null, ...)` is documented as legal ("body ... can be null"), but the constructor stored the `null` and `body()`, `charset()`, `isBinary()` and `length()` dereferenced it, so any body-less `Request` built outside `RequestTemplate` threw a `NullPointerException` on first access (the reproducer in #1210).

* The constructor now normalises a `null` body to `Request.Body.empty()`, the same default `RequestTemplate` already uses. `Body.empty()` yields exactly the documented contract — `body()` and `charset()` return `null`, `isBinary()` is `true`, `length()` is `0` — so clients that branch on `request.body() != null` (ApacheHttpClient, Logger, Vertx, ...) keep working unchanged. This follows the direction from the review of #1237: keep `body()` returning `null` for "no body" rather than an empty array.
* `toString()` checks the body's bytes instead of the (no longer nullable) wrapper, so a body-less request still prints only the request line and headers.
* Two tests in `RequestTest` pin the contract; CHANGELOG entry added under 13.17.

One intentional, visible side effect: a body-less request built through `RequestTemplate` previously printed a trailing `Binary data` line from `toString()` (because `RequestTemplate` already defaults to `Body.empty()`, whose `asString()` returns `"Binary data"`). With this change it prints only the request line and headers. No test asserted the old output, and `Logger` builds its own output.
